title: OpenSRM
description: Everything OpenSRM measures, grouped by subsystem. Panels are generated from scripts/build_dashboard.py — edit that file, not this JSON.

panels.title: Who uses it
panels.description: New vs returning vs total people, and how long a visit lasts. Read left to right: how many came, did they stay, what did they touch. People appear as a short hash — never a netid.

panels.title: How many new people?
panels.description: First-time users: accounts whose very first activity was in the last 24h and in the last 7 days. This is the growth number — a steady zero while total stays flat means nobody new is arriving.

panels.title: How many came back in 24h?
panels.description: People who used the app in the last 24h and are NOT first-timers. New + returning = everyone active in that window, so if the two do not add up to the active number, something is misclassified.

panels.title: How many accounts exist?
panels.description: Accounts, and how many of those have synced at least once. When they are EQUAL every account is working, which is the normal healthy state; when the synced count falls behind, those accounts signed up and never finished a first sync — the most expensive kind of dropout.

panels.title: How many are active?
panels.description: Distinct people in three windows. The sources differ on purpose: 'right now' is live in-process activity, while the 24h and 7d numbers are read from the event table. Right after a deploy the live count can briefly read lower than 'active in 24h' — that is a restart artefact, not a contradiction.

panels.title: When are people using it?
panels.description: How many distinct people were active each hour. The shape of this curve decides when to run a sync, a push, or a deploy without annoying anyone.

panels.title: What are people doing?
panels.description: Every event the app records, split by type, named in plain words rather than by the internal event id.

panels.title: How long does a visit last?
panels.description: From someone's first click to their last, with a 30-minute idle gap ending a visit. The median is a typical sitting; the 90th percentile is the long-visit tail — people keeping the app open, which is good provided the page is not slow.

panels.title: Which tabs do people open?
panels.description: Tab switches per hour, one line per tab — the legend names each tab. Tabs are a client-side switch, so this is the only evidence a tab is used at all; a tab that never appears here is dead weight in the navbar.

panels.title: What do people click inside a tab?
panels.description: Clicks on the real controls: expanding a marks component, opening a semester, hitting refresh. A control that never fires is either undiscoverable or unwanted — both are answers, and both are worth knowing before building more like it.

panels.title: Is anyone using it far more than others?
panels.description: Events per person per hour, top 8. One person far above the rest is usually a stuck client reloading, not enthusiasm.

panels.title: Logged-out traffic
panels.description: Events with no user attached: prefetches, bots, expired sessions. A jump here with real users flat means something is scanning the site.

panels.title: How long people wait
panels.description: Two completely different waiting experiences live behind the word 'sync'. A first login fetches everything cold and is slow by nature; a refresh by someone already signed in should be near-instant (it is usually answered from the last sync). This row keeps them apart on purpose.

panels.title: How long does a first login take?
panels.description: How long a fresh login takes, end to end, including the browser-driven portal fetch. This is the first impression — if the 95th percentile here is above about 30s, people are giving up before they see their data.

panels.title: How long does a refresh take?
panels.description: Answered from the last sync (should be milliseconds), waiting on a sync already running for the same account, or a real round trip. If the cache line is not the fastest, caching is not working.

panels.title: How often is a refresh answered instantly?
panels.description: The share of refresh requests that cost the portal nothing. Higher is better for both speed and the portal's rate limit — a drop here means the cache window is being missed by real traffic patterns.

panels.title: Where the sync time goes
panels.description: The portal (JSP pages over HTTP) and SCOPE (SOAP) are separate upstreams with separate failure modes. Keeping them apart is what makes 'the sync is slow' answerable — it is nearly always ONE of them.

panels.title: Which part of a sync is slow?
panels.description: Median seconds each part of a sync costs. The portal should dominate; writing to SQLite should be milliseconds. A persist line climbing means the disk is the problem, not the network.

panels.title: Where does the wait come from?
panels.description: The same thing as a proportion: what fraction of a person's wait is the portal, SCOPE, and disk. Quote this number, not the total, when arguing about where to optimise.

panels.title: Which SCOPE operation is slowest?
panels.description: Every SOAP operation by median cost. Five ops dominate a run (personal details, subjects, hourwise attendance, credit status, exam details) while the rest are sub-second — a new name appearing high on this list is upstream drift worth reacting to.

panels.title: Do SCOPE operations succeed?
panels.description: ok vs error per operation. Errors clustered on ONE op is that endpoint misbehaving; errors across all of them is the session or the network.

panels.title: SCOPE ops per sync
panels.description: How many SOAP ops a SCOPE run touched: none (everything fresh), 1-3, or 4+. High counts mean the cached SCOPE data keeps going stale.

panels.title: Storage and freshness
panels.description: How much room the data takes, how big one person's footprint is, and how stale the freshest data in the system is. A frozen timestamp here explains every 'nothing is updating' report before you read a log.

panels.title: How big is one person's data?
panels.description: The distribution of per-account storage (attendance, marks, subjects, SCOPE blobs and photo together). A synced student sits around 50-80KB today; an account far to the right is one whose SCOPE blob is bloated, and the 4MB bucket should stay empty.

panels.title: How stale is the data?
panels.description: Seconds since the freshest data in the whole system. If sync age climbs past a day while the app looks healthy, nobody is syncing — that is the difference between a quiet product and a broken one.

panels.title: Is the database growing?
panels.description: WAL size, event count and account count over time. The current file size is the 'DB size' tile in the infrastructure section; this shows the TREND. Usage events are retention-managed (365d): growth faster than adoption means pruning stopped.

panels.title: Errors people hit
panels.description: Who is failing and on what. Broken down by the route rule (never the raw path — a path carries a netid) and by event type, so one person's broken login can be told apart from everyone's.

panels.title: Who is hitting errors?
panels.description: Error events per person per hour. One name going up alone is that account's credentials; every name going up together is the portal or the network.

panels.title: Which pages fail?
panels.description: HTTP 5xx per route rule. The route name is the rule pattern (/api/login), never the URL, so this cannot leak who hit it.

panels.title: Which pages are slow?
panels.description: 95th-percentile latency per route. Sync routes legitimately run seconds; a static page in this list is a real problem.

panels.title: Liveness
panels.description: Is the app answering, is the scheduler ticking, how big is the process.

panels.title: Scrape up
panels.description: 1 = Prometheus reached /internal/metrics. 0 means the app is down OR the metrics token no longer matches METRICS_SECRET — check the secret file before assuming a crash.

panels.title: Push tick age
panels.description: Seconds since the every-minute tick last succeeded. >300s means the Hermes cron job is dead, disabled, or the host is gone.

panels.title: Portal cooldown
panels.description: Seconds the portal budget is still locked out. Non-zero means syncs are being refused for everyone right now.

panels.title: Process RSS
panels.description: Resident memory. A number that only climbs across days is a leak; the container limit is the ceiling to watch.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Gunicorn runs --threads 8; a number pinned at the ceiling means requests are queuing.

panels.title: DB size
panels.description: srm.db on disk. Growth is fine, a step change means a retention path stopped pruning.

panels.title: HTTP requests
panels.description: Every request, by matched route. This is the view that answers "what is the app actually being asked to do".

panels.title: Requests per minute by status class
panels.description: Throughput split by 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx. A 5xx bump here is the fastest signal that a deploy broke something.

panels.title: Latency p50 / p95 / p99 across all routes
panels.description: Server-side request duration. The sync-bearing routes (/api/refresh, /api/login) legitimately run seconds; a jump on a static route is the interesting case.

panels.title: Top routes by request rate
panels.description: Which routes carry the traffic. Cardinality is bounded by the route table, so this cannot explode.

panels.title: Top routes by p95 latency
panels.description: The slowest routes over the window. Expect the sync paths here; anything else is a regression.

panels.title: Errors by route (5xx only)
panels.description: Only 5xx. 4xx is dominated by bad logins and bot 404s and would drown the signal.

panels.title: Unmatched requests (24h)
panels.description: Requests for paths no route handles — scanners, stale bookmarks, or a frontend calling a removed API. A sudden jump usually means a deploy removed a route that clients still call.

panels.title: Portal syncs
panels.description: The scrape pipeline: outcomes, error taxonomy, duration, and the drift signals that mean the portal changed its markup.

panels.title: Syncs per minute by pipeline and outcome
panels.description: ok vs error per pipeline (http / playwright). Playwright is archived behind a flag, so it should be flat zero.

panels.title: Error classes (1h)
panels.description: The typed error vocabulary: bad_credentials, rate_limited, portal_cooldown, busy, portal_down, markup_changed, internal, auth, captcha, other. One class dominating names the cause.

panels.title: Sync duration p50 / p95
panels.description: End-to-end sync time. The pipeline deadline is 150s; p95 approaching it means users are timing out.

panels.title: Cache hits vs joined vs real syncs (1h)
panels.description: How much work single-flight and caching is saving. cached/joined should dwarf real syncs; if they do not, every user is paying full scrape cost.

panels.title: Parse-empty by page (24h) — portal drift
panels.description: A page parsed to zero records. Alive-empty is legitimate for seasonal pages (exams outside their window); a page that is normally populated going empty is the earliest markup-drift signal.

panels.title: Scrape-lock rejections
panels.description: A second scrape for the same user while one is in flight. Sustained rejections mean users are double-tapping refresh or a client is retrying too aggressively.

panels.title: Captcha attempts per login
panels.description: Average OCR attempts to clear the login captcha. A rising average means the captcha images are getting harder or the OCR model is degrading.

panels.title: Preflight fates (1h)
panels.description: The captcha pre-warm pipeline: ready / consumed / wasted / busy / failed. A high 'wasted' share means we are pre-warming sessions nobody uses; 'failed' means the pre-warm is not landing.

panels.title: SCOPE SOAP backend
panels.description: The SRMIST-SCOPE SOAP API: per-operation call rate, outcomes and latency. Faults here never affect the portal pipeline, but they surface as empty tabs.

panels.title: Calls per minute by operation
panels.description: Which SOAP ops drive traffic. A single op jumping is usually a page retry loop.

panels.title: Outcome split (1h)
panels.description: ok / http_error / transport_error. transport_error means the SOAP host was unreachable or timed out; http_error means it answered with a fault.

panels.title: Latency p50 / p95 by operation
panels.description: SOAP round-trip time. The client timeout is 15s; anything near it is about to start failing.

panels.title: Fault rate by operation
panels.description: Share of calls that were not ok. A single op at a high fault rate points at a contract change on that op.

panels.title: Push notifications
panels.description: Delivery attempts against the browser push services. Dead subscriptions accumulate here before any user complains.

panels.title: Delivery outcomes (1h)
panels.description: ok / retryable / dead / deadline / error. 'dead' is a 404/410 — the subscription is gone and gets deleted. 'deadline' means the tick ran out of time and deferred the send.

panels.title: Send latency p50 / p95
panels.description: Time inside pywebpush. The per-send timeout is 5s, so p95 near 5 means the push services are hanging.

panels.title: Delivery success rate
panels.description: ok / all attempts. A drop here with a flat request rate means the push services changed behaviour.

panels.title: Push tick throughput (1h)
panels.description: Ticks that completed ok vs errored. One per minute is expected; a gap shows up as fewer 'ok' bars.
